stories.title: Ajay's Luckiest Moment
stories.description: Ajay recounts how he returned to India in 1993 after his PhD, just as the economic reforms were starting. By 'dumb luck', he got involved with the team building the National Stock Exchange (NSE), which became a defining part of his career.

stories.title: Amit's Biggest Mistake
stories.description: Amit reflects on his early career, admitting he didn't work hard enough and lacked self-reflection. He was 'floating in his head', relying on talent rather than building processes and habits. He realized too late that 'youth is wasted on the young'.

stories.title: Tracy Chapman's Big Break
stories.description: The story of how Tracy Chapman got to perform 'Fast Car' at the Nelson Mandela Tribute Concert in 1988. Stevie Wonder had a technical issue and couldn't perform, so Chapman, who was just hanging around with her guitar, filled the slot. Her album sales went from 200k to 2 million in two weeks.

stories.title: The Starbucks Serendipity
stories.description: Amit shares how he met Vaibhav (of Chalchitra Talks) at a Starbucks in Versova. This chance meeting led to Amit later asking Vaibhav for crew recommendations, which resulted in hiring the current crew (Vaishnav and Namsita) for the podcast.

stories.title: Ajay's Father and CMIE
stories.description: Ajay recalls his father starting CMIE in 1976 and going out every day to meet people and campaign for his project, embodying the Sanskrit proverb 'Charati Charato Bhagha' (good things happen to those who move).

stories.title: Linus Torvalds
stories.description: Ajay uses Linus Torvalds as an example of someone who committed to a craft (writing the Linux kernel) without any guarantee of reward, money, or fame, driven purely by passion.

core_ideas.description: Luck isn't just random; you can increase the likelihood of it happening. The formula is: Luck = Passionate Doing (Excellence) x Effective Telling (Exposure). You need to build the craft AND put yourself out there.
A Sanskrit proverb meaning 'Good things happen to those who move'. Action and outreach are essential for serendipity.

A critique of the Indian mindset where people want a guaranteed reward (job, salary, status) before they commit to doing the work. True excellence comes from devotion to the craft without preconditions.
Doing things well brings joy, which fuels more work (virtuous cycle). Entitlement and seeking validation without work leads to bitterness and mediocrity (vicious cycle).
In an ideal 'six degrees' world, you only need to tell one person. In reality, there is 'transmission loss' in communication. Building a culture of trust and low resentment reduces this loss.
Using Malcolm Gladwell's terms: Mavens are deep experts (like Amit/Ajay), Connectors are people who link others (like Vaibhav). You can try to be both, or partner with the other type.
We can shape the culture of our elite networks to be less envious and more supportive, which makes the 'world' smaller and more efficient for ideas to travel.
